camb-087.title: The Jiangshanian extinction
camb-087.text: Diversity had just recovered when it fell again. After the recovery at the start of the Jiangshanian, a new extinction cut species diversity by 55.2%. Small fluctuations in species richness followed and lasted until shortly after the Ordovician began. The Furongian is divided into the Paibian, the Jiangshanian and the unnamed 10th stage of the Cambrian. The base of the Jiangshanian is marked by the first appearance of Agnostotes orientalis.

camb-092.title: The earliest brittle stars
camb-092.text: The earliest brittle stars (ophiuroids) appear about 488 Ma. The group contains two large clades, Ophiurida (brittle stars) and Euryalida (basket stars). Over 2,100 species in 256 recognized genera live today, which makes Ophiuroidea the most diverse and abundant echinoderm class.

ordo-007.title: The seas turn to calcite
ordo-007.text: The chemistry of seawater shifted. Mixed aragonite–calcite seas of the Cambrian gave way to fully calcite seas by the early Ordovician, though the change was not simple but protracted and variable through the Cambrian. Calcite seas coincided with times of rapid seafloor spreading and global greenhouse climate. Hardgrounds were very common in calcite seas such as those of the Ordovician and Jurassic, but virtually absent from the aragonite seas of the Permian.

ordo-017.title: The Sauk Sea retreats from North America
ordo-017.text: At its peak the shallow Sauk Sea had covered most of North America. With each sea-level rise, a shallow tropical ocean spread over most of the continent. Then a marine regression ended the Sauk sequence early in the Ordovician. The Tippecanoe sequence followed later in the period.

ordo-043.title: The Hunic terranes split from Gondwana
ordo-043.text:
A strip of continent tore away from Gondwana. Back-arc spreading split the Hunic terranes from it in the late Ordovician, opening the Paleo-Tethys Ocean, and the terranes began moving north toward Euramerica. Paleo-Tethys lay between Gondwana and the Hunic terranes, continental fragments that broke off and moved north.

The Hunic terranes are divided into the European Hunic (crust under parts of Europe, called Armorica, and Iberia) and the Asiatic Hunic (crust of parts of southern Asia). In the Early Carboniferous a subduction zone developed south of the European Hunic terranes, consuming Paleo-Tethys oceanic crust.

ordo-045.title: The last agnostid trilobites
ordo-045.text: Agnostids declined sharply across the Cambrian–Ordovician transition, and the last died out in the Late Ordovician. The Ordovician mass extinction ended them and the once-successful Telephinidae. It hit trilobites as a whole hard. They survived it, but went extinct in the end-Permian mass extinction.

ordo-062.title: Beecher's Trilobite Bed: soft parts in gold
ordo-062.text: A thin shale bed in Oneida County, New York, preserves trilobites such as Triarthrus eatoni with their soft tissues intact. It ranks among the world's best examples of near-perfect fossil preservation. The detail comes from pyritization, in which soft tissues are replaced with pyrite. In these trilobites the mineral pyrite, FeS2, has replaced the hard parts that made up the animal.

silu-003.title: The asaphid trilobites die out
silu-003.text: Asaphida, a large and varied trilobite order known since the Middle Cambrian, died out during the Silurian. The end-Ordovician extinction had reduced the diversity of all trilobite orders, with most asaphid families disappearing. Its last members, the Trinucleioidea, vanished before the end of the period. In 2020 the superfamily Trinucleioidea was proposed to be raised to an order, Trinucleida, and removed from Asaphida.

silu-011.title: The last dissidocerid cephalopods
silu-011.text: Dissidocerida, an order of orthocone cephalopods known since the Early Ordovician, last appears in the Early Silurian. Zhuravleva (1994) proposed the order for Dissidoceras undosum, a Silurian orthoconic genus with a wide, nearly central, tubular siphuncle, suborthochoanitic septal necks and an endosiphuncular rod.

silu-012.title: The last eocrinoids
silu-012.text: Eocrinoids, early stalked echinoderms known since Cambrian Stage 3, last appear in the Silurian. Cladograms show aspects of eocrinoid paraphyly or polyphyly, so the group's family tree is not a tidy single branch.

silu-013.title: The last nektaspid arthropods
silu-013.text: Nektaspida, unmineralised trilobite-like arthropods known since the early Cambrian, last appear in the upper Silurian. The youngest known nektaspid is the Laurentian naraoiid Naraoia bertensis from the Bertie Formation in Ontario, Canada, dating to the Upper Silurian.

silu-014.title: The last paracrinoids
silu-014.text: Paracrinoids lived in shallow seas from the Early Ordovician to the Early Silurian. Paracrinoidea is an extinct class of blastozoan echinoderms, and the Silurian marks its last appearance.

silu-016.title: Stromatoporoid sponges branch out
silu-016.text: Most stromatoporoid sponge orders, including Amphiporida and Stromatoporida, originated in the Silurian. Clathrodictyids and actinostromatids diversified strongly while labechiids declined. Amphiporida is first recorded in the Ludlow and lived from the mid-late Silurian (Wenlock or Ludlow) to the Late Devonian (Famennian). The order Actinostromatida may have originated earlier, in the Late Ordovician or the Llandovery Epoch of the early Silurian.

silu-019.title: The Rheic Ocean at its widest
silu-019.text: As Avalonia–Carolina drifted north from Gondwana, the Rheic Ocean reached its greatest width, about 4,000 km, in the Silurian. It separated Laurussia to the north from Gondwana to the south. The ocean existed from the Early Ordovician to the Early Carboniferous and was named after Rhea, sister of Iapetus. The Iapetus Ocean closed as Avalonia-Carolina collided with Laurentia and the Appalachian orogeny formed.

silu-033.title: The last bisonocerid nautiloids
silu-033.text: Bisonocerida, a nautiloid order dating from the Tremadocian, last appears in the Wenlock. When first defined as a new order, it was suggested to be an independent descendant of Ellesmerocerida. Bisonocerida was differentiated from Endocerida in 2012 to resolve this issue.

silu-039.title: The Great Glen Fault cuts across Scotland
silu-039.text: The Great Glen Fault formed late in the Caledonian orogeny, as Laurentia and Baltica collided, probably between 430 and 390 Ma. One source dates its start to c. 433 Ma. It shaped the Scottish Highlands. The fault had its final phase of movement during the Late Cretaceous to Early Tertiary. Much later, erosion along the fault zone during Quaternary glaciation formed Loch Ness.

silu-049.title: Palaeoscolecid worms make their final appearance
silu-049.text: Palaeoscolecids are extinct ecdysozoan worms resembling armoured priapulids. Known since the late Early Cambrian, they last appear in the Ludfordian, and the Lau event may have finished them off. They are mainly found as disarticulated sclerites, but are also preserved in many Cambrian lagerstätten. Their record runs from the Lower Cambrian to the lower Ludfordian.

silu-056.title: The oldest sac fungi
silu-056.text: The earliest known ascomycete fungi date from 423 to 419 Ma, in the Silurian. Dikaryan fungi, the group including ascomycetes, began expanding and diversifying then. Ascomycetes produce microscopic spores inside special elongated cells or sacs called asci, which give the group its name. Ascomycota is today the largest phylum of fungi, with over 64,000 species.

silu-059.title: Charcoal marks the first wildfires
silu-059.text:
Fire needs air with enough oxygen. In the Pridoli the first charcoal appears in the fossil record, so oxygen had first risen high enough for wildfires. Silurian charcoal shows oxygen had crossed about 15%, enough to sustain fire for the first time.

Fires were not yet routine. By the late Famennian, oxygen levels were high enough for wildfires to occur with regularity and on large scales, which had not been possible before because of the paucity of atmospheric oxygen.

silu-066.title: Ascocerid nautiloids vanish
silu-066.text: Ascocerida is an order of comparatively small nautiloids in the subclass Orthoceratoidea, known from Ordovician and Silurian sediments in Europe and North America. The end-Ordovician extinction cut them back, but they recovered in the Silurian. Then they died out abruptly at the end of the Silurian. A mature ascocerid, lacking its deciduous conch, would have been an effective swimmer.

devo-003.title: The Chaitenia arc docks with Patagonia
devo-003.text: An island arc named Chaitenia accreted to Patagonia, in what is now south-central Chile. Patagonia's margin turned convergent in the Devonian, leading to a collision that began in the mid-Carboniferous. The accretion is placed in the Devonian (c. 400–360 million years ago), inferred from an event of pressure, deformation and heating dated to that period. After Chaitenia merged, accretionary complexes developed to its west, so it acted as a backstop.

devo-008.title: The last of the radiodonts
devo-008.text: Radiodonts, the Cambrian predators that include Anomalocaris, make their last appearance in the Early Devonian. A late survivor was Schinderhannes bartelsi from Germany. They were among the earliest large predators, but also included sediment sifters and filter feeders. Until the 2010s they were considered uniformly large apex predators; new species discovered that decade greatly widened their known diversity.

devo-032.title: Lungfish and the dipnoan renaissance
devo-032.text: Lungfish appeared about 400 Ma and evolved rapidly through the Devonian, the 'dipnoan renaissance'. By the Middle Devonian (397-385 Ma) they had evolved proto-lungs and proto-limbs for spells outside water. Through convergent evolution, they also evolved internal nostrils similar to the tetrapods' choana. The first tetrapodomorphs, their closest kin, had the same general anatomy but appear not to have left the water until the Late Devonian.

devo-038.title: Forests cool the Middle Devonian
devo-038.text: Forests may have cooled the planet. Newly evolved forests drew carbon from the air and buried it in sediments, which may be reflected in a Middle Devonian cooling of around 5 °C. By the middle of the Devonian, several groups of vascular plants had evolved leaves and true roots. During the period free-sporing land plants spread across dry land, forming extensive coal forests that covered the continents.

devo-039.title: The progymnosperms appear
devo-039.text: Progymnosperms first appear in the Middle Devonian, and the group lasts into the Lopingian (late Permian). The oldest known belong to the Middle Devonian order Aneurophytales, with forms such as Protopteridium whose vegetative organs were relatively loose clusters of axes. Their order Archaeopteridales spans the Middle and Late Devonian. In the Late Devonian another group of progymnosperms gave rise to Archaeopteris, the first really large trees known.

devo-048.title: The Chilenia terrane docks
devo-048.text: Continued subduction led the Chilenia terrane to collide with and accrete to the western border of the Precordillera. Chilenia was an ancient microcontinent, or terrane, that affected many of the older rocks of central Chile and western Argentina. Another source dates its accretion to Cuyania, from which oceanic crust had separated it, to about 420–390 million years ago, when Cuyania was already joined to Gondwana.

devo-052.title: The Late Devonian warms again
devo-052.text: The Late Devonian warmed back to Early Devonian levels, shown by more continental weathering and plant distribution, without a matching CO2 rise. Arid climates became less widespread and temperate climates more common. Microbial reefs dominated under the warmer conditions of the early and late Devonian, while coral-stromatoporoid reefs dominated the cooler middle. The Devonian has been wrongly called a greenhouse age because of sampling bias: most early finds came from western Europe and eastern North America, which then straddled the Equator.

devo-055.title: Oxygen settles in the deep sea
devo-055.text: Deep-sea oxygen, sporadic and variable before, stabilized near modern levels only after 380 Ma. As plants took hold on the continental margins, oxygen levels increased and carbon dioxide dropped, although much less dramatically.

devo-057.title: The buried Kaluga crater
devo-057.text: An impact in what is now Kaluga Oblast, Russia, left a crater 15 km across, dated to 380 ± 5 Ma in the Late Devonian. It now lies buried under about 800 m of sediment and is not exposed at the surface. For eroded or buried craters, the stated diameter usually refers to an estimate of the original rim diameter and may not match present surface features.

devo-059.title: The Ilyinets crater
devo-059.text: The Ilyinets crater, in Vinnytsia Oblast, Ukraine, is 8.5 km across and formed about 378 ± 5 Ma. It lies at the boundary of the Ros–Tikych and Dniester–Bug megastructures of the Ukrainian Shield.

devo-070.title: Cladoselache, an early shark
devo-070.text: Cladoselache, an early shark and the first abundant genus of cartilaginous fish, appears about 370 Ma. It lived in the Late Devonian (Famennian) of North America and is one of the best-known early Chondrichthyes. Its cladodont teeth had a large sharp central cusp surrounded by one or two pairs of smaller cusps. It is often called the earliest shark in broad ecological terms, though it is only distantly related to modern sharks.

devo-076.title: Tadpole shrimps, living fossils
devo-076.text: The oldest known notostracan, Strudops goldenbergi, comes from the Famennian of Belgium, about 365 Ma. Notostracans are 2–5 centimetres long, with a broad carapace at the front and a long, slender abdomen. They are omnivores living on the bottom of temporary pools and shallow lakes. Living Triops and Lepidurus are 'living fossils', with similar forms since the end of the Devonian.

devo-077.title: The Woodleigh impact structure
devo-077.text: The Woodleigh impact structure in Western Australia, 60-160 km across, is dated to 364 ± 8 Ma, Late Devonian to Early Carboniferous. Its age roughly matches the Late Devonian extinction. Its central uplift, interpreted as 20 kilometres in diameter, was first intersected by drilling in the late 1970s, but its significance as an impact structure was only realised in 1997. In the early 2000s the event was thought to date between 259 and 201 million years ago.

devo-080.title: The proposed Warburton twin impacts
devo-080.text: Two 10-km asteroids may have struck Australia's West and East Warburton Basins, leaving a 400-km impact zone. This is proposed, not confirmed: the craters remain hypothetical. The idea is that an asteroid or comet split into two main pieces and hit the Australian continent, then part of Gondwana. The East Warburton crater is adjacent to the West Warburton crater, which is also around 200 km in diameter. The basins have been linked to the Late Devonian extinction, c. 360 Ma.

devo-087.title: The chitinozoans vanish
devo-087.text: Chitinozoans are flask-shaped, organic-walled marine microfossils produced by an as yet unknown organism. These pelagic filter-feeders appear to have died out at the end of the Devonian, completely, during the Hangenberg Event; rare later finds may be reworked. Bambach (2006) estimated that 31% of marine genera died out in the last substage of the Famennian.

carb-007.title: Giant lobe-finned fish rule fresh water
carb-007.text: Non-tetrapod lobe-finned fish were the dominant predators of Carboniferous and Permian fresh waters. The largest known, Rhizodus hibberti from Great Britain, reached up to 6 m long. Lobe-finned fish have muscular limb buds (lobes) within their fins, supported by appendicular skeletons. The clade declined significantly after the Permian-Triassic extinction event known as the Great Dying.

carb-008.title: The Granton Shrimp Bed
carb-008.text: This Scottish bed preserves Clydagnathus windsorensis, one of only three conodont species known with its trunk. Conodont elements are abundant, but fossils preserving the soft tissues of the animals are known from only a few deposits in the world. The elements are distinctive to particular species and are widely used in biostratigraphy to mark particular periods of geological time.

carb-010.title: The last cladoxylopsid trees
carb-010.text: Cladoxylopsids, large fern-ancestor trees, and their order Pseudosporochnales range from the Devonian to the Early Carboniferous. Early Carboniferous land plants were very similar to those of the Late Devonian, but new groups also appeared.
